title: Andrea needs to understand GenAI
message: One student’s learning process, from assignment to assessment
body: Andrea is a second-year computer science student: he can program, but still confuses key concepts of generative models.
He must study a chapter and explain how a small application generates text.
We observe his use of tools and the evidence of understanding he keeps.

title: What is self-directed learning?
message: Self-directed learning is a process in which learners take the initiative to identify learning needs, set goals, choose resources and strategies, and evaluate outcomes.

comparison.label: 1. Identify a goal
comparison.text: What do I need to learn, and what do I want to achieve?

comparison.label: 2. Choose a path
comparison.text: Which resources, people and strategies will help me learn?

comparison.label: 3. Evaluate progress
comparison.text: What have I learned, and what should I change? Self-assessment helps here.

result: “I need to distinguish training from inference. I will use the chapter and a concept map, then check whether I can explain the difference.”
decision: Teachers and peers can support the process; the learner takes responsibility for the choices.

title: What is self-assessment?
message: Self-assessment means judging your own work and learning against explicit criteria, then using that judgment to improve.

comparison.label: 1. Check the criteria
comparison.text: What should I be able to explain or do?

comparison.label: 2. Look for evidence
comparison.text: What can I demonstrate? Where do I still struggle?

comparison.label: 3. Choose a next step
comparison.text: What will I revise, practise or check again?

result: “I can explain what a token is, but I still confuse training and inference. I will revise that link in my map and explain it again.”
decision: AI can offer feedback; the learner checks the evidence and decides what to improve.

title: Assisted performance and learning
message: One study separates what happens during and after assistance
body: High-school mathematics, nearly 1,000 students in one Turkish school; not a trial of these tools.

comparison.label: With AI assistance
comparison.text: In Bastani and colleagues’ trial, assisted practice performance improved.

comparison.label: Later, without AI
comparison.text: The general-chat group performed below the control; instructional safeguards largely mitigated that harm.

decision: Workshop design choice: keep a brief independent assessment as well.

stage: ChatGPT · informal shortcuts applied to the book
title: /eli5 · Causal attention in plain language
message: Book §5 · The Transformer decoder
prompt: /eli5 Using only §5 of the attached book, explain causal attention to a 15-year-old in no more than 80 words. Explain which tokens a position can use, why future tokens are blocked and what happens after a token is generated. Keep the technical meaning. Answer in English.
result:
Causal attention is a mechanism that helps a Transformer language model predict the next token (a piece of text).
Each position can use information from earlier tokens and itself, but not from later positions. A causal mask blocks future tokens so the model cannot use information that should not yet be available.
Once a new token is generated, it is added to the sequence. The model can then use it to predict the next token, repeating the process.
decision: Use it to simplify an explanation while preserving the causal constraint.

stage: ChatGPT · informal shortcuts applied to the book
title: /mindmap · How a model generates text
message: Book §§2–7 · A text map with named relationships
prompt: /mindmap Using only §§2–7 of the attached book, create a text mind map centred on “Text generation”. Use five branches and label each relationship. Include tokens, decoder blocks, probabilities, generation and training. Distinguish parameter updates from ordinary inference. Answer in English. Keep the complete response within 100 words.
result:
TEXT GENERATION
Text generation
1. Tokens — are converted into numerical IDs, then embeddings with positional information.
2. Decoder blocks — transform representations using causal attention, allowing access only to current and earlier positions.
3. Probabilities — are calculated from logits through softmax; temperature changes their concentration.
4. Generation — selects and appends one token, then repeats inference until stopping.
5. Training — updates parameters to reduce prediction error; ordinary inference uses fixed parameters without updating them.
decision: Use it to organise the chapter; explain each link without looking at the map.

stage: ChatGPT · informal shortcuts applied to the book
title: /flashcard · Three distinctions to remember
message: Book §§2, 3 and 6 · Recall before checking the answer
prompt: /flashcard Using only §§2, 3 and 6 of the attached book, write exactly three question-and-answer flashcards. Test token versus word, context versus parameters, and token probability versus truth. Keep each answer under 30 words. Answer in English. Keep the complete response within 100 words.
decision: Answer the question before revealing the card; compare with the chapter.

media.alt: The actual ChatGPT flashcard widget, recorded while revealing three answers about tokens, context and probabilities.
media.caption: Actual ChatGPT output · recorded interaction
media.transcript:
1. How is a token different from a word? A token may represent a word, part of a word, punctuation, or spaces. Tokens and words are not equivalent.
2. How do context and model parameters differ? Context supplies information for current inference. Parameters are learned numerical values updated during training, not ordinary inference.
3. Does a token's probability indicate an answer's truth? No. It estimates how likely a token is as the next continuation, not whether the complete answer is true.

stage: ChatGPT · informal shortcuts applied to the book
title: /quiz · Check understanding of temperature
message: Book §6 · Probabilities and temperature
prompt: /quiz Using only §6 of the attached book, write three short questions about temperature at fixed logits. Test concentration, ranking and truth. Put a numbered answer key after the questions, with a brief reason for each answer. Answer in English. Keep the complete response within 100 words.
result:
Quiz: Temperature at Fixed Logits
1. Concentration: What happens to the probability distribution when temperature increases?
2. Ranking: Does increasing temperature change which token has the highest probability?
3. Truth: Does lowering temperature make the generated answer necessarily more truthful?
Answer key
1. Less concentrated. Higher temperature spreads probability more evenly across alternatives.
2. No. At fixed logits, temperature changes probabilities but preserves their ranking.
3. No. Temperature changes the probability distribution, not the model's knowledge or the truthfulness of its answers.
decision: Use the answer key after an independent attempt; investigate the reason for each error.

stage: ChatGPT · informal shortcuts applied to the book
title: /commonwrong · Correct two misconceptions
message: Book §§2, 6 and 8 · Find the error and explain the correction
prompt: /commonwrong Using only §§2, 6 and 8 of the attached book, show two common misconceptions: uploading a book trains the model, and lowering temperature removes hallucinations. For each, give the wrong claim and a correction with its reason. Answer in English. Keep the complete response within 100 words.
result:
1. Uploading a book trains the model
 Wrong claim: “Uploading a book updates the model’s parameters.”
 Correction: Uploading a book may provide information through context or retrieval. Only training or fine-tuning updates parameters; ordinary inference uses fixed parameters.
2. Lowering temperature removes hallucinations
 Wrong claim: “Lower temperature guarantees accurate answers.”
 Correction: Lower temperature concentrates probabilities on more likely tokens. It does not verify truth or eliminate hallucinations. Deterministic selection may repeatedly produce the same mistake.
decision: Use it to diagnose a misconception; ask the learner to justify the correction.

stage: ChatGPT · informal shortcuts applied to the book
title: /rubric · Assess the chapter assignment
message: Book §§9–10 · Evidence of the learner’s understanding
prompt: /rubric Using only §§9–10 of the attached book, create a 6-point formative rubric for Andrea’s assignment. Use three criteria worth 0–2 points each. Give a shared scoring scale and describe the evidence needed for full marks on each criterion. Assess understanding, not just working code. Answer in English. Keep the complete response within 100 words.
result:
Formative Rubric — 6 Points
Shared scale: 0 = absent/incorrect; 1 = partial understanding; 2 = complete, independently justified evidence.
Criterion — Full marks (2 points)
1. Conceptual understanding — Independently explain tokenization, probability calculation, sampling, and generation; connect functions to model behavior.
2. Experimental reasoning — Record two controlled experiments, predict outcomes, change one variable, and interpret probability differences versus sampled outputs.
3. Critical evaluation — Identify a code or conceptual error, explain its cause, and demonstrate a test revealing it.
Total: 6 points. Working code alone is insufficient; understanding requires independent explanation, prediction, interpretation, and verification.
decision: Use the rubric for feedback, then ask for an independent explanation of one step.

title: Do skills improve results?
message: Two recent preprints show why the task and evaluation design matter.

comparison.label: SkillsBench · v4
comparison.text:
87 tasks · 8 domains · 18 model–harness configurations.
Average pass rate: 33.9% → 50.5% (+16.6 percentage points). Focused skill bundles performed better than exhaustive ones.

comparison.label: SWE-Skills-Bench · v2
comparison.text:
98 software-engineering skills · 4 agent–model configurations.
92 had no statistically significant effect. Average pass ratio: 76.6% → 76.9% (+0.3 percentage points).

decision: Different tasks and baselines: these figures do not rank this catalogue or measure student learning.

title: Choose a skill by the task
message: Practical selection criteria derived from the documentation and benchmark findings.

comparison.label: Strong candidate
comparison.text: A narrow recurring task, a clear input and output, maintained dependencies and checks that match the deliverable.

comparison.label: Weak candidate
comparison.text: Generic advice already supplied by the model, incompatible tools, changing external rules or long procedures unrelated to the task.

decision: Compare factual errors, missing requirements, usable output and effort with and without the skill.

steps.text: Ask a focused question, then check its reference to the chapter.

decision: A topic tree provides orientation; its relationships still need explanation.

title: Self-check before seeing the solution
message: Close the source, attempt an answer, then reopen it to revise
body: Andrea answers before reading a solution, then checks and records a correction.
prompt: Ask one question that distinguishes context from training. Do not reveal the answer immediately. After my attempt, identify one correct point and one to revise, with a chapter reference.
decision: A generated quiz is useful when it leads to an attempt and revision.

title: Excalidraw: revise the relationships
message: The second map makes the conceptual change visible

steps.title: Training
steps.text: Data → “contributes to updating” → parameters.

steps.title: Inference
steps.text: Context → “enters calculation with fixed parameters” → probabilities.

steps.title: Generation
steps.text: Distribution → “guides selection of” → next token.

decision: Read every arrow as a meaningful statement.

title: Compare the two map versions
message: The important change is in the explanation
body: Andrea identifies one correct relationship, one revision and one remaining uncertainty.

comparison.label: Before · teaching example
comparison.text: “Does context train the model again?”

comparison.label: After · expected explanation
comparison.text: “During inference, the calculation input changes without updating parameters”.

decision: The comparison prepares an independent explanation; it does not replace it.

title: Napkin: start with checked text
message: Choose the relationships before generating the visual
prompt: Training updates parameters. During inference, the context text becomes a token sequence. The model calculates probabilities for the next token. A selection rule chooses a token and the process repeats.

steps.title: Paste the text
steps.text: Use a summary checked against the chapter.

steps.title: Select and generate
steps.text: Request a visual for that specific passage.

decision: Napkin proposes a representation; it does not certify the text.

media.alt: Napkin: selected text and the blue Generate Visual control on its left.
media.caption: Generate control in the official guide; the vendor’s example text is unrelated to Andrea.

title: Choose and correct the visual
message: Prefer a representation that preserves the meaning

comparison.label: Avoid
comparison.text: One arrow labelled “prompt → training → answer” mixes different processes.

comparison.label: Look for
comparison.text: Separate training; show a cycle for token-by-token inference.

steps.title: Review labels and arrows
steps.text: Correct terms before choosing colours or icons.

steps.title: Justify the choice
steps.text: Explain why this representation expresses the process.

media.alt: Napkin interface showing alternative generated visual representations.
media.caption: Official guide: choosing a visual.

title: A diagram to use during the exercise
message: A short reference with explicit relationships
output: Export as PNG/PDF in the Free plan, keeping product branding.

steps.title: Text and context
steps.text: Are converted into tokens.

steps.title: Model with fixed parameters
steps.text: Processes the tokens and calculates a distribution.

steps.title: Selection and repetition
steps.text: A token is added; the context for the next step changes.

result: Export as PNG/PDF in the Free plan, keeping product branding.
decision: The learner must be able to explain the cycle in their own words.

title: The exercise: a small app with a real model
message: AI may write the solution; Andrea must be able to interpret it
body: Enter text and inspect its tokens.
Show five next-token alternatives, probabilities and remaining mass.
Change temperature and generate a short continuation.
Compare two tests and explain a difference.
decision: A real model in the browser, with no paid API.

title: Claude: a complete assignment
message: Specify material, behaviour and checks before generating code
body: A reusable teaching request, not the production log of the distributed code.
prompt: Create an English browser app using a real language model, without a paid API. Use Transformers.js and ONNX Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct q4. Show input tokens, five next-token alternatives with probabilities and remaining mass, temperature, and generation up to 24 tokens. Add comparison, reset, loading and error states. Distinguish the explanatory diagram from real data. Explain dependencies, limitations and checks. Use the attached chapter as the conceptual reference.
decision: A complete prompt defines the task; the solution still needs verification.

title: Open and check the solution
message: A ready interface begins the study of the exercise
body: Kit provenance: application developed with Codex. The Claude prompt lets you repeat the task.

steps.title: Run it
steps.text: Load the model and actually generate a token.

steps.title: Check the data
steps.text: Probabilities use the full vocabulary; show the remaining mass.

steps.title: Keep the revisions
steps.text: Record corrections, runtime and model version.

decision: A plausible result does not replace a functioning test.

title: A designed tutor can support learning
message: Positive findings concern specific tasks and conditions

comparison.label: Designed tutor · Kestin 2025
comparison.text: An RCT with 194 university physics students found better immediate outcomes with the studied tutor than the comparison active class.

comparison.label: Guided use · Huang 2026
comparison.text: With 95 students, structured training improved AI-assisted revision of electromagnetism problems.

decision: Workshop choice: ask for attempts, source checks and revision; then assess independence.

title: From input to the first token
message: Observe real data in a short test

steps.title: Enter the text
steps.text: Use a short input and record it.

steps.title: Read the tokens
steps.text: Inspect the actual segmentation: tokens do not necessarily match words.

steps.title: Calculate and generate
steps.text: Compare alternatives and remaining mass, then generate a single token.

decision: Percentages concern token selection; they do not measure a statement’s truth.

media.alt: Real local model run, comparing the same context at two temperatures and then changing context.
media.caption: Recorded local inference · Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct q4 · English captions and transcript in the kit.
media.transcript:
REAL RECORDING — local inference Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct q4

00:00:00.000  I load the real model from this computer. No remote API is used.

00:00:04.366  I analyze the starting text. Tokens and probabilities come from the model.

00:00:07.695  I save A, then change only temperature, from 0.8 to 1.5.

00:00:10.206  Probabilities spread out; the most likely token keeps its top rank.

00:00:12.700  Now I change context: France instead of Italy. Temperature returns to 0.8.

00:00:16.153  I sample one token from the full vocabulary. The generated text joins the context.

00:00:19.308  I generate a short continuation. I can stop subsequent steps.

00:00:24.959  I reset the results. The model stays loaded in memory.

00:00:27.394  Real recording. High probability does not mean a true fact.

title: The process represented by the app
message: An explanatory diagram, separate from the calculated values

steps.title: Input and tokens
steps.text: Text is encoded as a sequence.

steps.title: Representations and position
steps.text: Numbers and order information enter the model’s blocks.

steps.title: Transformer blocks
steps.text: Causal attention and transformations process the available information.

steps.title: Distribution and selection
steps.text: Scores become probabilities; selection adds the next token.

decision: This diagram explains a flow; it does not reveal the model’s thoughts.

title: Change the context, keep the model
message: A recorded comparison with the same model and temperature
body: Recorded local inference, 1 November 2026. Only the initial context changes.

comparison.label: Context A · T = 0.8
comparison.text: “The capital of Italy is” → next-token candidate “ Rome”: 44.86%.

comparison.label: Context B · T = 0.8
comparison.text: “The capital of France is” → next-token candidate “ Paris”: 91.23%.

decision: These are conditional token probabilities, not factual-accuracy percentages.

title: Temperature changes the distribution
message: Recorded run · identical input and logits, two temperature settings
body: Input: “The capital of Italy is”. Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct ONNX q4; local CPU/WASM run.

comparison.label: T = 0.8 · more concentrated
comparison.text: “ Rome”: 44.86%; remaining vocabulary outside the top five: 26.51%.

comparison.label: T = 1.5 · less concentrated
comparison.text: “ Rome”: 8.06%; remaining vocabulary outside the top five: 79.96%.

decision: Temperature changes this distribution; it adds no knowledge and does not guarantee truth.

title: Read the formula from the chapter
message: Softmax with temperature · identify the role of each symbol

steps.title: zᵢ · score
steps.text: A number calculated by the model for candidate token i.

steps.title: T · temperature
steps.text: A positive setting that rescales scores before conversion.

steps.title: pᵢ · probability
steps.text: The exponentiated score divided by the sum over all candidates.

decision: The denominator makes the probabilities sum to one. Probability is not truth.

title: A short symbol guide
message: Read the notation before asking for another explanation

steps.title: i and j · candidates
steps.text: i identifies the candidate being considered; j runs over all candidates in the denominator.

steps.title: exp(a) · a positive weight
steps.text: This means e raised to a. Apply it to each score divided by the positive temperature.

steps.title: Σ · add the weights
steps.text: Sum all candidate weights, then divide each weight by this common total.

decision: The three-candidate example shows the same arithmetic on a deliberately small vocabulary.

title: Notebook: ask about the formula
message: Explain the symbols, check the source, then make a prediction
prompt: Use the chapter’s softmax-with-temperature formula. Explain each symbol and the denominator in three short steps. Distinguish a score from a probability. Work through scores [2, 1, 0] at T = 1 and show the sum. Then ask me to predict the effect of increasing T, and wait for my answer.
decision: Check the cited passage and the arithmetic; an explanation generated by AI still needs review.

title: Desmos: make the formula observable
message: Three invented scores for a worked example, separate from the real model

steps.title: Open the free calculator
steps.text: Use the copy-ready expressions in the kit. Here x is temperature T > 0.

steps.title: Compare fixed scores
steps.text: Read the three curves at x = 0.5, 1 and 2. Change temperature while keeping scores [2, 1, 0].

decision: Desmos plots and evaluates the entered mathematics; it does not explain the chapter automatically.

media.alt: Desmos plots the three softmax probabilities for illustrative scores [2, 1, 0]. The horizontal axis is temperature from 0 to 4; the vertical axis is probability from 0 to 1.
media.caption: Real Desmos graph · invented scores for the worked example, separate from Qwen measurements.

title: Check the worked example numerically
message: Fixed scores [2, 1, 0] · probabilities rounded to four decimals
body: Before rounding, each distribution sums to 1. Higher T makes these fixed-score probabilities less concentrated.
decision: Ask Andrea to explain why the ranking stays the same while concentration changes.

title: Notebook: study the solution
message: Connect one application function to a chapter concept
body: Add a textual solution description, including version and provenance, alongside the chapter.
prompt: Use the chapter and the solution description. Explain the transition from scores to probabilities in three steps. Identify its connection to the chapter. Then ask me what would change with a higher temperature, without giving the answer.
decision: Andrea reconstructs the step, returning to the code or source when needed.

title: What Andrea must demonstrate independently
message: An explanation, a prediction and an error correction

steps.title: Explain
steps.text: Describe how context contributes to generation.

steps.title: Predict
steps.text: Justify the expected effect of changing temperature.

steps.title: Correct
steps.text: Refute “The most probable token always provides true information”.

steps.title: Reflect
steps.text: Identify one useful support and one remaining uncertainty.

decision: A brief attempt without chat; then reopen materials to revise mistakes.

title: The teacher designs the evidence
message: The goal, task and criterion must concern the same knowledge

comparison.label: Goal
comparison.text: Understand the roles of context, parameters and token selection.

comparison.label: Evidence
comparison.text: An explanation, commented diagram, justified prediction and correction.

comparison.label: Criteria
comparison.text: Concepts and relationships; process explanation; application and checking.

decision: Assess what the learner can justify, alongside the assisted product.

title: MagicSchool: draft a rubric
message: The teacher provides goals, assignment and constraints
prompt: Prepare a rubric for the attached assignment. Three criteria: concepts and relationships; process explanation; application and checking. Four levels with observable descriptors. Assess GenAI knowledge, without rewarding only polished prose or code. Distinguish the assisted product from the independent explanation.

steps.title: Open Rubric Generator
steps.text: Enter goals and assignment, without learner personal data.

steps.title: Generate a draft
steps.text: Check it against the chapter before using it.

title: Review the rubric descriptors
message: A constructed revision example, not automated assessment
body: Keep three criteria separate and apply the same rubric to the responses.

comparison.label: Too general
comparison.text: “Shows a good understanding of the topic”.

comparison.label: Observable
comparison.text: “Distinguishes parameters from context and explains why changing a prompt is not retraining”.

decision: The rubric stays in the kit without Formative’s paid integrated rubric feature.

title: Rubric: concepts and relationships
message: Criterion 1 · four levels of evidence

steps.title: 1 · Needs reconstruction
steps.text: Confuses training and inference, or treats probabilities as truth.

steps.title: 2 · Partial
steps.text: Names concepts, but incompletely relates parameters and context.

steps.title: 3 · Coherent
steps.text: Distinguishes phases and states correct relationships.

steps.title: 4 · Justified
steps.text: Justifies relationships and identifies conditions and limits in a new example.

decision: Apply the criterion to meaning in the agreed response mode.

title: Rubric: process explanation
message: Criterion 2 · make the links between stages explicit

steps.title: 1 · Absent
steps.text: Repeats output without describing the stages.

steps.title: 2 · Fragmentary
steps.text: Describes some stages but leaves gaps or reversals.

steps.title: 3 · Ordered
steps.text: Connects input, tokens, processing, distribution and selection.

steps.title: 4 · Justified
steps.text: Explains the links and separates the diagram from observed data.

decision: A commented diagram or oral explanation can reveal the same process.

title: Rubric: application and checking
message: Criterion 3 · predict, test and revise

steps.title: 1 · Unjustified
steps.text: States a conclusion without a prediction or check.

steps.title: 2 · Incomplete
steps.text: Predicts, but changes multiple conditions or does not compare outcomes.

steps.title: 3 · Controlled
steps.text: Varies one condition, compares the outcome and corrects an error.

steps.title: 4 · Critical
steps.text: Justifies revision and recognises sampling, limitations and uncertainty.

decision: Do not reward a lucky outcome from one generation.

title: Prepare questions and expected answers
message: The first question checks a fundamental distinction
body: Q1 · During ordinary inference, what changes when a new prompt is entered? A: original training data. B: calculation context. C: learned parameters.
Expected: B, with justification; a correct choice alone provides limited evidence.
prompt: Generate five chapter-based questions: distinction, explanation, diagram, prediction and transfer. For each, provide the expected answer, a detectable misconception and the rubric criterion. Avoid questions answered by copying a definition.
decision: A teacher-reviewed teaching example, not a validated test.

title: Explanation and diagram completion
message: Questions 2 and 3 · observe the connections

comparison.label: Q2 · Explain
comparison.text: Why does a token not always match a word? Expected: encoding may split words or represent other sequence elements.

comparison.label: Q3 · Complete a diagram
comparison.text: Complete text → tokens → model → distribution → selection. What repeats? Expected: the selected token joins the context and calculation continues.

decision: Read correctness and explanation without requiring code.

title: Prediction and transfer
message: Questions 4 and 5 · apply a concept and recognise an error

comparison.label: Q4 · Predict
comparison.text: Same input and scores: what changes from T = 0.5 to T = 1.2? Expected: less concentrated probabilities, without a guarantee about one sampled token.

comparison.label: Q5 · Correct an error
comparison.text: “The most probable alternative will be true”. Refute using a new example. Expected: token plausibility differs from content truth.

decision: Keep the initial prediction, test outcome and justified revision.

title: Formative: set up the assessment
message: One collection point, with clear instructions and available criteria

steps.title: Create the activity
steps.text: State the goal and when materials are allowed or chat must be closed.

steps.title: Add five questions
steps.text: Use multiple choice, open response and drawing in the Free plan.

steps.title: Prepare the review
steps.text: Key for Q1; teacher review for explanations and diagrams.

decision: Use the standalone kit rubric; no premium integration is needed.

media.alt: Formative: opening the Responses view for an assessment; vendor example.
media.caption: Official guide screenshot; vendor example data.

title: Choose the format for the evidence
message: Three response types, three opportunities to observe

comparison.label: Multiple choice + reason
comparison.text: Identify a distinction and inspect the reasoning.

comparison.label: Open response
comparison.text: Observe explanations, predictions and corrections.

comparison.label: Drawing + commentary
comparison.text: Make the sequence and relationships visible.

decision: Integrated audio/video responses are paid features; agree alternatives when needed.

title: Read three simulated responses
message: Invented examples for discussing teacher judgement

comparison.label: Profile A · complete product
comparison.text: The app works, but the explanation says every prompt updates parameters.

comparison.label: Profile B · vocabulary present
comparison.text: Names tokens and probabilities, but omits the link between distribution and selection.

comparison.label: Profile C · coherent explanation
comparison.text: Distinguishes phases, justifies a prediction and recognises the limit of one generation.

decision: Read differences criterion by criterion before summarising with a grade.

title: Feedback that specifies the next action
message: Teacher-written examples address the observed difficulty

comparison.label: For profile A
comparison.text: Revisit parameters versus context. Correct the arrow and explain why.

comparison.label: For profile B
comparison.text: Add the selection rule between distribution and token. Explain the link.

comparison.label: For profile C
comparison.text: Transfer your explanation to a new context and identify what remains uncertain.

decision: Teacher-written feedback in the Free plan, followed by a new learner attempt.

title: Activity: adapt an assessment
message: Five minutes on your subject and an access barrier

steps.title: Choose a goal · 1 minute
steps.text: Name a concept you teach or study.

steps.title: Design evidence · 2 minutes
steps.text: Write a task and observable criterion, allowing AI to produce the initial product.

steps.title: Remove a barrier · 2 minutes
steps.text: Offer an equivalent access or response option; share the reason for your choice.

decision: A reusable example with a coherent goal, evidence and support.

title: Accessibility and learning differences
message: Start with the barrier in the actual task, with the learner

comparison.label: Reading and fatigue
comparison.text: Adaptable text, read aloud, segments and pauses.

comparison.label: Writing the response
comparison.text: Dictation, review or another agreed response mode.

comparison.label: Organisation and calculation
comparison.text: A visible plan, glossary, diagrams and goal-aligned supports.

decision: Dyslexia and other specific learning difficulties vary; attention needs are distinct. No typeface or tool fits everyone.

title: Edge: another way to read the same chapter
message: Access to the text and understanding require separate checks

steps.title: Open the chapter HTML
steps.text: Use Reading mode on a supported page or selected passage.

steps.title: Adapt and listen
steps.text: Try text preferences and Read aloud; adjust the speed.

steps.title: Check usefulness
steps.text: Pause at the paragraph and explain the relationship you read.

decision: Read aloud supports access; understanding still needs a learner attempt.

media.alt: Official Microsoft Edge Reading mode screenshot, highlighting the Read aloud command in the toolbar.
media.caption: Official Microsoft guide: Read aloud control; vendor example content unrelated to Andrea.

title: Notebook: short segments and a glossary
message: Adapt presentation while checking that meaning is preserved
body: Compare each segment with the original; choose the appropriate detail with the learner.
prompt: Rewrite this paragraph in three short segments. Define token, context and parameters. Preserve the condition “during inference” and flag each simplification. Do not remove essential relationships.
decision: A brief explanation helps when it preserves the concept’s conditions.

title: Dictation: express and review an answer
message: Speech produces text that the learner must check

steps.title: Configure Dictation
steps.text: On Mac: System Settings → Keyboard → Dictation; choose language and activation.

steps.title: Dictate into the answer field
steps.text: Explain the role of context.

steps.title: Read and revise
steps.text: Check technical terms, negations and punctuation before submitting.

decision: Windows offers voice typing; check availability and settings on the actual device.

title: An accessible assessment of the same goal
message: Change the mode while preserving the evidence sought
body: Goal: explain the generation process, rather than writing speed.
Possible agreed responses: reviewed text, oral explanation or commented diagram.
Clear instructions, advance criteria and supports aligned with the task.
decision: Apply the same conceptual criteria, using response arrangements appropriate to the educational context.

title: Reuse the learning path in another subject
message: Keep the sequence; change the content and evidence

steps.title: Start with a source and a goal
steps.text: For example: understand a historical interpretation from an assigned chapter.

steps.title: Make ideas visible
steps.text: Record an initial explanation, uncertainties and a manageable plan.

steps.title: Use tools, then check
steps.text: Compare a generated explanation with the source and revise relationships.

steps.title: Demonstrate and reflect
steps.text: Explain a new example independently; identify the next learning step.

decision: Choose a tool for a specific need and decide what evidence it should leave.

title: The evidence collected along the way
message: A product and an explanation answer different assessment needs

comparison.label: Learning process
comparison.text: Initial map, selected plan, checked passage and revised map.

comparison.label: Assisted product
comparison.text: Diagram, application, recorded tests and revision history.

comparison.label: Demonstrated knowledge
comparison.text: Independent explanation, prediction, error correction and reflection.

decision: Compare these records before deciding what the learner needs next.
